subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 16! In this unit you will become an expert on chance – the special part of maths that helps us talk about how likely something is to happen. Chance is all around you, every single day. When Amina wonders whether it will rain before she reaches the masjid, when Yusuf flips a bottle cap to decide who kicks off the football match, or when Halima guesses which goat will reach the water trough first, they are all thinking about chance.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use the words certain, likely, even chance, unlikely and impossible correctly.
Place events on a probability scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Write a simple probability as a fraction, and know it can also be a decimal or percentage.
Work out the probability of an event using favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
Compare two events using more likely than, less likely than and equally likely as.
Tell the difference between a fair experiment and an unfair (biased) one.
Carry out a chance experiment, record results neatly, and find the experimental probability.
Predict how many times an event should happen using probability × number of trials.

concepts.title: The Language of Chance
concepts.explanation:
Chance is a way of describing how likely something is to happen. Before we use any numbers at all, we describe chance with words. There are five words that matter most in this unit, and you should learn them like old friends.

Certain – it will definitely happen. There is no doubt at all.

Likely – it will probably happen, but we cannot be completely sure.

Even chance – it is just as likely to happen as it is to not happen.

Unlikely – it will probably not happen, but it just might.

Impossible – it can never happen, no matter what.

Let us make each word real with an example from daily life. It is certain that night will follow day. It is likely that the market in Hargeisa will be busy on a normal morning. There is an even chance that a flipped bottle cap lands the right way up. It is unlikely that Omar will find a camel wandering in his classroom. And it is impossible for a goat to drink the whole sea dry.

Notice how these words go in an order, from least likely to most likely: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain. Picture them as five steps on a staircase. At the very bottom step sits 'impossible' – no chance at all. At the very top sits 'certain' – full chance. Right in the middle is 'even chance', where the event is balanced perfectly, just as likely to happen as not. Learning this order is the foundation of everything else in the unit.
concepts.example: A common trap catches many learners here, so let us clear it up straight away. Unlikely does not mean impossible. An unlikely event still *can* happen – it just does not happen very often. It is unlikely that Zahra rolls a 6 on her first try, but it is certainly possible; it happens roughly one time in six. In the same way, likely does not mean certain. A likely event usually happens, but not always. Keeping these two ideas separate is one of the most important things you will learn in this whole unit.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale from 0 to 1
concepts.explanation:
Words are useful, but mathematicians also like to measure chance with numbers. We do this on a special number line called the probability scale. It runs from 0 to 1, and every chance in the world fits somewhere on it.

0 means the event is impossible. It has no chance at all.

1 means the event is certain. It will definitely happen.

one half (0.5) means an even chance – exactly in the middle.

Anything between 0 and one half is unlikely (a low chance).

Anything between one half and 1 is likely (a high chance).

Picture the probability scale as the road from Mogadishu to Hargeisa, with 'impossible' at the start and 'certain' at the end. The exact middle of the road is the 'even chance' resting place. If an event is only a short way along the road, it is unlikely. If it is far along, close to the end, it is likely. This picture helps you *see* how big a chance is, and how two chances compare.

The same chance can be written in three different clothes, and they all mean exactly the same thing. We can write a probability as a fraction (such as one quarter), as a decimal (such as 0.25), or as a percentage (such as 25%). In Year 3 we will mostly use fractions and simple words, because fractions show the maths most clearly, but it is good to know that a weather forecaster who says '25% chance of rain' is talking about the very same one-quarter chance.
concepts.example: Let us place a few events on the scale to practise. 'The sun will rise' sits right at 1 (certain). 'A normal die shows a 7' sits right at 0 (impossible). 'A coin lands on heads' sits at the middle, one half (even chance). 'It will rain in the dry season' sits low down, close to 0 (unlikely). 'A ripe mango will fall from a heavy tree in a strong wind' sits high up, close to 1 (likely). Every event has its own home on the scale.

concepts.title: Working Out Simple Probabilities
concepts.explanation:
When every outcome is equally likely, we can work out an exact probability with a simple rule. This is one of the most useful ideas in the whole unit, so read it slowly:

⭐ The Probability Rule Probability = number of favourable outcomes divided by total number of possible outcomes. A favourable outcome is simply the result we are hoping for or asking about.

Let us see the rule in action with a six-sided die. A die has six faces: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. That means there are 6 possible outcomes in total, and on a fair die each is equally likely. Now we can answer many questions:

Probability of rolling a 3: only one face shows 3, so it is 1 out of 6, written as one sixth.

Probability of rolling an even number (2, 4 or 6): three faces are favourable, so 3 out of 6, which simplifies to one half.

Probability of rolling a number less than 5 (1, 2, 3 or 4): four faces are favourable, so 4 out of 6, which simplifies to two thirds.

Probability of rolling a 7: no face shows 7, so 0 out of 6, which is 0 – impossible.

Notice the pattern: we count how many outcomes are favourable (the top of the fraction), then how many outcomes there are altogether (the bottom of the fraction). The die never lies – as long as it is fair, these fractions are exactly right.

The rule works for anything with equally likely outcomes, not just dice. Imagine a bag holding 3 red marbles, 2 blue marbles and 5 green marbles. Altogether there are 3 + 2 + 5 = 10 marbles, so there are 10 possible outcomes when you draw one without looking. The probability of drawing a red marble is 3 out of 10 (three tenths). The probability of drawing a blue marble is 2 out of 10, which simplifies to one fifth. The probability of drawing a green marble is 5 out of 10, which is one half. And the probability of drawing a marble that is not green is 5 out of 10 as well, because five of the marbles (the reds and blues together) are not green.
concepts.example: Here is a lovely shortcut that will save you time again and again. The probability that an event does not happen is found by taking the probability that it does happen away from 1 (the whole). If the chance of drawing a green marble is one half, then the chance of *not* drawing green must be 1 minus one half, which is also one half. If the chance of rain is one quarter, the chance of no rain is three quarters. The whole always adds up to 1, because something must happen.

concepts.title: Comparing How Likely Events Are
concepts.explanation:
Often we do not need an exact fraction – we just want to know which of two events is more likely. To compare events we use three handy phrases:

More likely than – this event has a bigger chance than that one.

Less likely than – this event has a smaller chance than that one.

Equally likely as – the two events have exactly the same chance.

Let us compare some die rolls. Rolling a 6 (chance one sixth) is less likely than rolling an even number (chance one half), because one sixth is smaller than one half. Rolling an even number is equally likely as rolling an odd number, because each has three favourable faces out of six. And rolling a number greater than 2 is more likely than rolling a number less than 2, because four faces beat one face.

A neat way to compare is to write both chances as fractions with the same bottom number, then simply look at the tops. Rolling a 6 is 1 out of 6; rolling an even number is 3 out of 6. Because 3 is bigger than 1, the even number wins. Whenever the bottoms match, the fraction with the bigger top is the more likely event. This is the same skill you use when comparing any fractions, now put to work on chance.
concepts.example: Comparing chances helps us make good decisions in real life. If Farah is choosing which game to play at the Eid fair, and one game gives her a one-half chance of winning a prize while another gives only a one-tenth chance, she can see at a glance that the first game is the better bet. Being able to compare likelihoods is what turns chance from a mystery into a tool you can actually use.

concepts.title: Fair and Unfair Chance Experiments
concepts.explanation:
A chance experiment is any activity with more than one possible result, where you cannot say for sure what will happen each time. Flipping a coin, rolling a die, spinning a spinner, and drawing a marble from a bag are all chance experiments. The single results – heads, or a 4, or a red marble – are called outcomes, and each go of the experiment is called a trial.

Experiments can be fair or unfair. In a fair experiment, every outcome has an equal chance of happening. A fair coin gives heads and tails each a one-half chance. A fair six-sided die gives every number a one-sixth chance. A fair spinner has equal-sized sections. Fairness is what makes our probability rule work perfectly.

In an unfair (also called biased) experiment, some outcomes are more likely than others. A coin that has been bent might land on heads far more often than tails. A spinner with one huge section and three tiny sections is unfair, because the pointer will stop on the big section much more often. When Hassan builds a spinner for a class game, he must check that the sections are equal, or the game will not be fair to everyone.
concepts.example: Why does this matter? Because in maths, the neat fractions we calculate – like one sixth for a die – only hold true when the experiment is fair. If someone hands you a die and it keeps landing on 6, you should become suspicious that the die is unfair. Knowing the difference between fair and unfair keeps you a careful, honest mathematician.

concepts.title: Experimental Probability
concepts.explanation:
So far we have worked out chances by thinking – this is called theoretical probability, because it comes from the theory, or the idea, of the experiment. But we can also find a probability by actually doing the experiment many times and counting what happens. This is called experimental probability.

⭐ Experimental Probability Rule Experimental probability = number of times the outcome happened divided by the total number of trials. The more trials you do, the closer your experimental probability usually gets to the theoretical one.

Suppose Maryam flips a coin 20 times and counts 11 heads and 9 tails. Her experimental probability of heads is 11 out of 20. The theoretical probability of heads is one half, which would be 10 out of 20. Her result of 11 is very close to 10, but not exactly the same – and that is completely normal. Chance wobbles a little each time you try it.

Here is the exciting part. If Maryam kept flipping – 100 times, then 1000 times – her experimental probability would creep closer and closer to the theoretical one half. This idea, that more trials give a more reliable result, is one of the deepest truths about chance. It is why doctors test medicine on many people, not just one, and why weather forecasters study many past days, not just yesterday.
concepts.example: Real workers use experimental probability all the time. A factory that makes water bottles in Nairobi might test 100 bottles from a huge batch. If 3 of the 100 leak, the experimental probability of a leaky bottle is 3 out of 100. The factory can then predict that about 3 in every 100 bottles in the whole batch might leak, and fix their machines before too many are wasted. Chance turns a small test into useful knowledge about a very large group.

methods.title: How to work out a probability
methods.example: Which word best describes this event: 'A normal die will land on a number from 1 to 6'?
steps: Count the favourable outcomes (the results you want).
Count the total number of possible outcomes.
Write the fraction: favourable over total.
Simplify the fraction if you can (3 out of 6 becomes one half).

methods.title: How to find an experimental probability
methods.example: Where does 'A flipped coin lands on tails' sit on the probability scale?
steps: Do the experiment many times and tally the results.
Count how many times your outcome happened.
Write it over the total number of trials.
Remember: more trials usually give a result closer to the theoretical probability.

methods.title: How to make a prediction
methods.example: What is the probability of rolling an odd number on a fair six-sided die?
steps: Find the probability of the event as a fraction.
Multiply that fraction by the number of trials.
State the answer as 'about' — the real result will wobble around it.

methods.title: A marble bag
methods.example: A bag has 4 red, 3 blue and 3 yellow marbles. What is the probability of drawing a blue marble?
steps: First find the total: 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 marbles.
Blue marbles are favourable: there are 3 of them.
So the probability is 3 out of 10 (three tenths).

methods.title: The 'not' shortcut
methods.example: Using the same bag (4 red, 3 blue, 3 yellow), what is the probability of drawing a marble that is not red?
steps: The probability of red is 4 out of 10.
Something must happen, so the whole is 1, which is 10 out of 10.
Take red away: 10 − 4 = 6.
So 'not red' is 6 out of 10, which simplifies to three fifths.

methods.title: Compare two events
methods.example: Which is more likely on a fair die: rolling a 2, or rolling a number greater than 4?
steps: Rolling a 2 is 1 out of 6.
Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so that is 2 out of 6.
Both have the same bottom number, and 2 is bigger than 1, so rolling a number greater than 4 is more likely.

workedExamples.title: Choose the right chance word
workedExamples.prompt: Which word best describes this event: 'A normal die will land on a number from 1 to 6'?
workedExamples.solution: Every face of a die shows a number from 1 to 6, so this event always happens. It is certain, with a probability of 1. There is no way for the die to land on anything else.

workedExamples.title: Place an event on the scale
workedExamples.prompt: Where does 'A flipped coin lands on tails' sit on the probability scale?
workedExamples.solution: A coin has two equally likely outcomes, heads and tails. Tails is one of the two, so its probability is one half. That sits exactly in the middle of the scale — an even chance.

workedExamples.title: Work out a die probability
workedExamples.prompt: What is the probability of rolling an odd number on a fair six-sided die?
workedExamples.solution: The odd numbers on a die are 1, 3 and 5 — that is 3 favourable outcomes. There are 6 outcomes in total. So the probability is 3 out of 6, which simplifies to one half. Rolling an odd number is an even chance.

workedExamples.title: A marble bag
workedExamples.prompt: A bag has 4 red, 3 blue and 3 yellow marbles. What is the probability of drawing a blue marble?
workedExamples.solution: First find the total: 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 marbles. Blue marbles are favourable: there are 3 of them. So the probability is 3 out of 10 (three tenths).

workedExamples.title: The 'not' shortcut
workedExamples.prompt: Using the same bag (4 red, 3 blue, 3 yellow), what is the probability of drawing a marble that is not red?
workedExamples.solution: The probability of red is 4 out of 10. Something must happen, so the whole is 1, which is 10 out of 10. Take red away: 10 − 4 = 6. So 'not red' is 6 out of 10, which simplifies to three fifths. (Check: blue 3 + yellow 3 = 6. It matches!)

workedExamples.title: Compare two events
workedExamples.prompt: Which is more likely on a fair die: rolling a 2, or rolling a number greater than 4?
workedExamples.solution: Rolling a 2 is 1 out of 6. Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so that is 2 out of 6. Both have the same bottom number, and 2 is bigger than 1, so rolling a number greater than 4 is more likely.

workedExamples.title: Experimental probability
workedExamples.prompt: Khadija flipped a coin 50 times and got 28 heads and 22 tails. What is the experimental probability of heads?
workedExamples.solution: Heads happened 28 times out of 50 trials, so the experimental probability is 28 out of 50. This is a little more than one half (which would be 25 out of 50), but close — exactly what we expect from a fair coin over 50 flips.

workedExamples.title: Make a prediction
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, green and yellow. If you spin it 40 times, about how many times should it land on blue?
workedExamples.solution: Blue is 1 of the 4 equal sections, so the probability of blue is one quarter. Expected times = one quarter of 40 = 10 times. You might get 8 or 12 in real life, but about 10 is what to expect.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: The chance of an event is three tenths. What is the chance it does not happen?
workedExamples.solution: does not happen = 1 − three tenths = seven tenths.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, red, blue, yellow. What is the probability of landing on red?

workedExamples.title: Say whether each experiment is fair or unfair
workedExamples.prompt: Say whether each experiment is fair or unfair: a) a coin that lands heads 9 times out of 10, b) a normal six-sided die, c) a spinner with equal sections.
workedExamples.solution: a) unfair (biased), b) fair, c) fair.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: A fair die is rolled 60 times. Predict about how many times each number should appear, and explain why the real result might be different.
workedExamples.solution: 1) Each number: probability one sixth, so expect 60 ÷ 6 = 10 times each; real results wobble because chance varies from trial to trial.

activities.title: The Coin-Flip Experiment
activities.materials: a coin, paper and a pencil.
steps: Before you start, predict: how many heads do you think you will get in 20 flips?
Flip the coin 20 times. Make a tally mark for heads or tails each time.
Count your heads and tails. Write the experimental probability of heads as 'heads out of 20'.
Compare it to the theoretical probability of one half (which would be 10 out of 20). How close were you?
If you have time, do another 20 flips and add them to the first. With 40 flips, is your result closer to one half? This is the law that more trials give a more reliable answer.

activities.title: Roll and Tally (Die Investigation)
activities.materials: a die, paper and a pencil.
steps: Draw a tally chart with a row for each number 1 to 6.
Roll the die 30 times, making a tally mark for each result.
Count the tallies. Which number came up most? Which came up least?
The theoretical chance of each number is one sixth (about 5 times in 30). How do your results compare?
Ask yourself: does this mean the die is unfair, or is this just the normal wobble of chance? Discuss your idea with a family member.

activities.title: Make a Marble Bag
activities.materials: a bag or cup, and 10 small objects in different colours (beans, stones or bottle caps).
steps: Put in 5 of one colour, 3 of another, and 2 of a third. Write down how many of each.
Work out the theoretical probability of drawing each colour as a fraction.
Draw one object without looking, record its colour, then put it back. Repeat 20 times.
Compare your experimental results to the fractions you calculated. Are they close?

activities.title: Build a Spinner and Test Fairness
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a small stick or matchstick for the pointer.
steps: Draw a circle and divide it into 4 equal sections. Colour them red, blue, green and yellow.
Push the stick through the centre so it can spin.
Predict the chance of landing on each colour, then spin 40 times and tally the results.
Now draw an *unfair* spinner with one big section and three tiny ones. Predict how the results will differ, then test it.

activities.title: Chance Word Sort (Family Game)
activities.materials: small slips of paper and a pencil.
steps: On five slips, write: certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible. Lay them out in order.
Each player thinks of a real event and says it aloud – for example, 'It will rain today.'
Everyone points to the slip that best matches the event, and you discuss any disagreements.
Keep score: a point for each event you and a partner label the same way.

activities.title: Prediction Challenge (Investigation)
activities.materials: a die, paper and a pencil, and other people if possible.
steps: Predict how many times you will roll a 6 in 30 rolls. (Hint: the chance of a 6 is one sixth.)
Roll the die 30 times and count your 6s. Compare to your prediction.
If you have a group, add everyone's rolls together. With, say, 150 rolls in total, how many 6s appeared?
Is the big group's result closer to the prediction than your own 30 rolls? Talk about why.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand chance best? Were your experimental results close to the theoretical probabilities, or did they wobble? What surprised you most? Why do more trials give a more reliable answer? Share your thoughts with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: The Probability Scale 0 = impossible. 1 = certain. One half = even chance. Every probability is between 0 and 1 – never less than 0, never more than 1.

rules.title: The Probability Rule
rules.text: Probability = favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. Example: rolling an even number on a die = 3 out of 6 = one half.

rules.title: The 'Not' Rule
rules.text: Probability an event does NOT happen = 1 minus the probability it does. If rain is one quarter, then no rain is three quarters.

rules.title: The Prediction Rule
rules.text: Expected number of times = probability multiplied by number of trials. Example: a 4 on a die over 60 rolls = one sixth of 60 = about 10 times.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Maryam flipped a coin 40 times and got 17 heads. Find her experimental probability of heads, and say whether the coin seems roughly fair.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 17 out of 40; one half would be 20 out of 40, so 17 is a little below but close – the coin seems roughly fair.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A bag has 12 marbles. It is certain you will draw a marble, it is unlikely you draw yellow, and red and blue are equally likely. Give one possible number of each colour and explain your reasoning.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: One possible answer: 5 red, 5 blue, 1 green, 1 yellow (total = 12) - red and blue are equal, and yellow is unlikely at 1 out of 12; other answers are possible as long as red equals blue and yellow stays small.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A spinner has 8 equal sections numbered 1 to 8. Use chance words to describe: a) spinning an even number, b) spinning a number greater than 6, c) spinning a number less than 9.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: a) Spinning an even number (2, 4, 6 or 8) is 4 out of 8, which is an even chance. b) Spinning a number greater than 6 (7 or 8) is 2 out of 8, which is unlikely. c) Spinning a number less than 9 is certain, since every number from 1 to 8 is less than 9.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Fair and Unfair Chance Experiments.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A chance experiment is any activity with more than one possible result, where you cannot say for sure what will happen each time. Flipping a coin, rolling a die, spinning a spinner, and drawing a marble from a bag are all chance experiments. The single results – heads, or a 4, or a red marble – are called outcomes, and each go of the experiment is called a trial.

Experiments can be fair or unfair. In a fair experiment, every outcome has an equal chance of happening. A fair coin gives heads and tails each a one-half chance. A fair six-sided die gives every number a one-sixth chance. A fair spinner has equal-sized sections. Fairness is what makes our probability rule work perfectly.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Experimental Probability.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
So far we have worked out chances by thinking – this is called theoretical probability, because it comes from the theory, or the idea, of the experiment. But we can also find a probability by actually doing the experiment many times and counting what happens. This is called experimental probability.

⭐ Experimental Probability Rule Experimental probability = number of times the outcome happened divided by the total number of trials. The more trials you do, the closer your experimental probability usually gets to the theoretical one.

questions.explanation: The sun rising tomorrow will definitely happen, so it is certain.

questions.question: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What fraction of the marbles are red?
questions.hint: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
questions.explanation: There are 10 marbles in total, and 3 are red, so the probability is 3 out of 10, written as the fraction 3/10.

questions.question: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 5?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: There is 1 favourable outcome (rolling a 5) out of 6 possible outcomes, so the probability is 1/6.

questions.question: Which is more likely on a fair die: rolling an even number, or rolling a 6?
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Outcome" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: Rolling an even number (2, 4 or 6) is 3 out of 6, but rolling a 6 is only 1 out of 6, so an even number is more likely.

questions.question: A coin lands on heads 19 times out of 20 flips. Is this most likely a fair or an unfair coin?
questions.hint: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
questions.explanation: A fair coin should land on heads about half the time. Landing on heads 19 out of 20 times suggests the coin is biased.

questions.question: Yusuf rolls a die 30 times and records: 6 ones, 4 twos, 5 threes, 6 fours, 4 fives, 5 sixes. What is his experimental probability of rolling a 4?
questions.hint: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
questions.explanation: He rolled a 4 six times out of 30 trials, so the experimental probability is 6 out of 30 (which simplifies to one fifth).

questions.question: A spinner has 5 equal sections, one of which is green. If you spin it 100 times, about how many times should it land on green?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: Green is 1 of 5 equal sections, so the probability is one fifth. Expected times = one fifth of 100 = 20.

rounds.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a 5?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: There is 1 favourable outcome (rolling a 5) out of 6 possible outcomes, so the probability is 1/6.

rounds.prompt: Yusuf rolls a die 30 times and records: 6 ones, 4 twos, 5 threes, 6 fours, 4 fives, 5 sixes. What is his experimental probability of rolling a 4?

rounds.explanation: He rolled a 4 six times out of 30 trials, so the experimental probability is 6 out of 30 (which simplifies to one fifth).

selfAssessment: I can use the words certain, likely, even chance, unlikely and impossible correctly.
I can place events on a probability scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
I can write a simple probability as a fraction, and know it can also be a decimal or percentage.
I can work out the probability of an event using favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
I can compare two events using more likely than, less likely than and equally likely as.
I can tell the difference between a fair experiment and an unfair (biased) one.
I can carry out a chance experiment, record results neatly, and find the experimental probability.
I can predict how many times an event should happen using probability × number of trials.
